newsitem.title: USA: Heating oil prices tumble as stock rebuilding begins.
newsitem.headline: Heating oil prices tumble as stock rebuilding begins.

text.p: Heating oil prices tumbled Wednesday after an industry report on Tuesday indicated stockpiles may be rising from record lows.

"The key here is that high refinery rates and production levels could result in stocks rebuilding pretty rapidly," said Ken Miller, senior principal at Purvin & Gertz Inc, an international energy consulting firm.
Heating oil for November delivery settled fell 2.49 cents to 70.96 cents a gallon at the New York Mercantile Exchange.
The selling weighed on crude oil and gasoline.
December crude oil fell 67 cents to $24.86 a barrel and November gasoline lost 0.96 cent to 68.16 cents a gallon.

The American Petroleum Institute (API) reported on Tuesday that heating oil stocks grew by 2.4 million barrels last week, with much of the increase coming in the Northeast, the biggest market for heating oil in the world.

Heating oil prices have risen steeply in recent months as inventories sank to record lows. The API report said distillate stocks overall, including diesel and heating oil, were about unchanged for the week ended Oct. 18.
But traders said record distillate production rates of 3.7 million barrels a day was a sign heating oil stocks would rise further.
Meanwhile, Colonial Pipeline Co. on Monday said it received a surge in requests to ship distillates, especially heating oil, on its huge pipeline that runs from Houston to the New York Harbour.
"Basically this means that there is plenty of barrels of distillate available to be shipped to the Northeast," said Linda Abramo, analyst with Energy Security Analysis Inc.
The Commodity Research Bureau's index of 17 commodities fell 0.85 points to 244.11.
Elsewhere, soybean prices rose on persistent rumours of Chinese buying and harvest delays in key growing areas in the Midwest.

"There was follow through-buying on talk of China business. Also not just rain but snow fell in some areas (of the Midwest) and that got some attention," said Mark Cermak of Chicago-based grain house O'Connor and Co.
Traders said there was talk that China had bought 50,000 metric tons of domestic soybeans this week and were looking to buy another 50,000 tons.
November soybeans rose 9-1/2 cents to $6.98-1/2 a bushel at the Chicago Board of Trade.
Platinum rose despite weakness in other precious metals, with sentiment buoyed by signs of strength in the auto industry, a big consumer of the metal.
"Automobile production is looking healthy which supports demand for platinum group metals in emissions control devices," CPM Group analyst Edward Kemp said.
January platinum rose $1 to $391.90 an ounce after touching a two-week high of $392.40.
Silver and gold in contrast were slightly weaker. December silver fell 0.2 cents to $4.988 an ounce and December gold lost 20 cents to $385.90 an ounce, both at New York's Commodity Exchange.
